projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Norton Norr was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War Two Veteran, Norton Norr. Mr. Norr served in the U.S. Army Force with the 8th Air Force. His highest rank was the staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Norr's apartment in Cleveland Heights, Ohio on March 20, 2003. Norton was 82 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: In 1941, I was living over at Anistale 3623 Anistale Which was across from the park off of Taylor Road.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, when I went into the service, I think I was about 21.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It was in 1942.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you still -- let's see. You probably were working maybe in 1941?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. I was working down town at the Old Higbee Company. I was in their Complaint Department. I was very, very lucky. I got a job. I originally started work up in their warehouse up on the 10th floor. I knew where everything was in the building, and when they needed an assistant in the Complaint Department, they went to me because I knew where everybody was in the building. And I was one of these guys that always kept people happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I can't recall.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Back at Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I remember that day and I was -- I can tell you where I was living, on 125th Street. I remember hearing it on the radio, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then, were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Not actually, because my brother had a child and they called me in. They first called him in and they drafted him, and then they called me in and they said, if I want to enlist now, then they wouldn't take my brother because if there's somebody in the family that's in, they won't take a parent with a child. So I enlisted and he didn't have to go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you did that for your brother?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's very nice.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, he had a child at the time. I was married but I had no children, so, and I was going to be taken in anyhow, so I figured this would help him stay home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As long as you went in first, they didn't take him?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That's right. And I would have gone in anyhow, so I was no big hero.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But it's still nice you went in a little sooner.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What branch of the service was that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I was in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what about did you go in?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I was with -- actually, I was with Air Transport Command. At that time, it was all one Air Force and now everything is all split up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the army __...(two seconds).

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see. When did you go in, then? It was sometime in the middle of '42?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, June something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, the training was all down the Keesler Field. Actually, it originally started up in Wisconsin, then down the Keesler Field. And then they shipped me out west and after three days, they shipped me all the way back east, and they broke us up in different -- some of us got summer clothes, some of us got winter clothes. We said goodbye to each other and we all wound up on the same ship. The crazy Air Force. I don't know how they figured these things out. I guess they're trying to confuse the enemy, but they confused more than that. We all lined up on the same ship and wound up in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the Army Air Corp your first choice?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No. It was just -- it was just available at that time, and they put me there. They didn't ask questions. They sent you here, they sent you there. Whenever they wanted to. Wherever they needed you, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that's the way it worked when they signed up, whoever needed people at that point?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You couldn't necessarily --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, I enlisted because if I didn't, my brother would have been taken.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: And he had a child, and then I would have been taken anyhow because I had no children at the time. I was married, but no children.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other unusual stories about your training?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: The training, yeah, was very good. We were three days out. They shipped us all the way out up to Wisconsin and then from Wisconsin they shipped us out west for three days and they shipped us back to Virginia, and they gave me winter clothes and gave my buddies summer clothes and said goodbye to each other and all wound up on the same ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was it like during your training being thrown in with a bunch of guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, it was interesting because we were all younger at the time and none of us were really worried about things. And we got to see parts of the country we had never seen before and we took advantage of it. At least I was one of the few guys that did. The other guys all sat around playing cards or drinking or something like that, but as long as I was out west, and I had never been there before, I took advantage of it. The same thing wherever I was in the world. I was in a lot of places.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you visit when you were out west?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Visit?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of places did you go to?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, we were outside of Salt Lake City. There was an army base, but we were only there about a week. So we got into Salt Lake City for one day, but that was about it. Then we were shipped all the way back east, and the next thing we know, they had gave me winter clothes, they gave my buddies summer clothes and we all wound up on the same ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was that crossing? When did you make the crossing?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It took an about a month by ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And would this be 1942?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, by boat. And we went all the way around. We were outside of Rio de Janeiro, but they wouldn't let us off the ship to go visiting because I think they were afraid some of them would disappear. Then we went all the way around, came up the Red Sea into Egypt. From there, we got into the desert.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that a good crossing a rough crossing or --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No. It was very interesting. The ocean was nice. The only time -- the thing that happened was exciting was we were -- I used to volunteer because we always got good food there and we didn't have to wait in line three or four hours to eat once, and then you dont eat again until six, seven hours later. So you only ate twice a day, but I volunteered to work in the kitchen. And they have a whole series of kitchens and we wound up in the ship's officers kitchen area, so we always got the best food and ate whenever we wanted to. So it was worth it to us, you know. They're always guys looking for ways not to work but we -- several of us that did that. We were always used to working because we worked before we went in. And it was worth it to us because we got whatever food we wanted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said that crossing took about a month?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: 46 days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 46 days?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We went all the way down out of Virginia. It was interesting. Some of us had winter clothes, some of us had summer clothes. So we got to where the ships were and we all said goodbye to each other because we know we were going north or going south. We all wound up on the same ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did the guys with winter clothes get summer clothes?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I don't know what -- wherever we landed, yeah, we got.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you got there?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Whatever we needed, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do -- when you weren't working, what did you do to pass the time on that long crossing?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I used to sit down on the deck below where they used to throw garbage out. But during the day, that deck was clean because they didn't want to dump stuff into the water where anybody could see it or follow it. So we used to sit out there. We worked during the day and we always got the best food because we worked there. And some of the guys were too lazy, would stand and wait in line for hours and hours to get two meals a day. So we figured to us it was worth it. There were a few of us, not too many guys. And we were always able to take showers in a special area that the other guys didn't know about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: On the boat?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I don't know. What kind of entertainment?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, card playing, music.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Oh, we played cards, that's all. Some of us played cards, not too often, yeah. But we enjoyed doing the work and keeping busy, so -- and then during the day, we'd sit out on that special deck where they threw garbage out. Well, during the day it was clean because they wouldn't throw any garbage out during the day. They only threw at night. So that was really very relaxing. The only exciting thing that ever happened there was we were sitting there one day and all of a sudden there was a big explosion, and all of us guys there wet our pants. We thought we were hit or killed. Turned out there was a navy crew up above us and they were practicing shooting. But they didn't do that for weeks until we were way out in the ocean and there was nobody anywhere near around. And they shot those things. We had no idea. We thought we were all being killed at one time. And they were about five guys of us and about four of us just wet our pants.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that your own anti-aircraft that was shooting, or was it a navy plane dropping a --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No, no, no. It was a navy, was on the ship and they were practicing shooting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Practicing shooting?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they cleaned out the guns or something.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That's right. They blew off of it and nobody told us about that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They didn't warn anybody?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. And we were on the deck below that where they used to tumble garbage off at night, but during the day it was clean. It was a beautiful spot to stay and very relaxing because we worked in that area. And to me, you know, there was several of us guys who felt we were better off working during the day than sitting and waiting in line to get food, and then coming back and waiting in line. We only had two meals a day, but here we were working, actually in an officer's mess kitchen, and we got all the the food we wanted. Any kind of food we wanted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any sub scares or anything when you crossed?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, the only thing was when that gun went off for practice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you didn't -- there weren't any submarine sightings or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was this a large convoy?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It was the SS Mariposa. It was a big ship that used to go from San Diego to Hawaii. It was a beautiful ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was a single ship that was making the crossing?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What output was this?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, at that time, I was in the Air Force Unit, but I didn't know where we were going or for what. I wound up in Egypt based outside of Cairo.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many guys were on that ship?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Oh, I have no idea. It was the SS Mariposa. It was a beautiful cruise ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was a cruise ship?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That used to go to Hawaii from -- but there were a lot of people on, I tell you. They wait in line twice a day for hours so they get the two meals. And that's one of the things -- reasons why some of us guys who weren't lazy figured we're better off working, getting whatever food we want, whenever we want it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you landed in Cairo?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We landed, not in Cairo but Port Suez. And then they -- well, actually, we were originally put out in the desert for two days and they they took us back on the ship and took us down to, I can't remember the name of the town where we got off, and took a train into Khartoum in the Sudan. And that took about a week or so. And then I was based there for a short while. And then I began flying there and my first flight, that's an interesting story, too. My first flight was to go from Khartoum down south, and there was a guy that was there two weeks before me and he was like a senior guy and this was all new to me, so he said, he'd like to take that trip and is that all right with me, he says. But he's going to take it whether it's all right with me or not. So I said, sure, go ahead. And I'm still here because he took that trip for me because that plane took off and crashed and they all got killed. So I was very fortunate. But he insisted on it, and at that time I could have said, no, I guess. But it was all new to me and I was afraid to say no to somebody especially that had a sergeant's ranking on him. I was a private so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they have engine trouble, or how -- why did they go down?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I happened to be there because I was going to get on a plane and he came up and he said, he's been there longer than me and he'd like to take that trip and so he's going to do it. So I said, okay. I didn't know anything. I'm not going to argue with anybody in the army. So they took off and they crashed on take-off. I happened to be at the airport at the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you saw it?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: From that point on, I never asked anybody to take their place or because there was a better trip than what I was scheduled on. Whatever I was assigned, I took it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So a little superstitious?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any good luck charms when you were flying?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I just never believed in stuff like that. I did what my job was and that was it. If it's my turn, it's my turn. That's the way I always felt and I still, to this day, I can't believe sometimes that why I'm still here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: There's DC-3s at that time.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: C-47 or C-54. When I came home after two years flying that whole Middle East area, they put me on C-54 engine and I made 13 roundtrips from New York to Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bringing troops back?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Taking stuff from people there to bringing people back, flying ambassadors to different areas, and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your position on that plane?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I was a Flight Radio Operator.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A Flight Radio Operator. How big was the crew on that plane?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We had a captain, co-captain, we had a navigator and we had a radio operator, but we never were over 10,000 feet, so the navigator never did anything because we were in the clouds all the time. I was doing all the work so I got to know where all the radio stations -- I was in contact with Africa and with England. I was the specialist. They used to say they couldn't go anywhere without me and I'd laugh because I didn't fly the airplane. But I did keep contact with -- I knew where everything was, the radio was, you know. But I wasn't the only operator. Any radio operator on the airplane knew where everything else was, and the navigators had nothing to do. We were in the clouds. We were never over 10,000 feet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what were your missions in North Africa? What were you doing mainly?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We originally started to fly shells for the British out of Cairo and the first place we'd go to would be like Tobruk which was a short -- we could make two, three trips a day to Tobruk and then, as they pushed the British back we'd fly a little bit further each time until we finally wound up at Benghazi and then later Tripoli. So that's what we started doing, and then later on after about two months, they called us in two planes, two crews, and they said we're putting you guys on special missions because you know where everything is around here. We all looked at each other and started to laugh. All we ever did was fly into the desert and back. We went a little further each time, started out on Tobruk and kept on going all the way up along, all the way until Tripoli. But then, from then on, I was all over the whole Middle East. We got into Turkey and Russia. Those were interesting trips because we had to go down and get civilian clothes because Turkey was a neutral nation and you couldn't walk in. They stripped our airplane and make airplanes their air company, had a name on it. I don't remember what it was. But we'd land up in turkey and Ankara and there was a German airplane come in with us civilians. And we see these guys skating off and their wearing not uniforms, but civilian clothes just like we did. We knew who they were and they knew who we were, but we never talked to them, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things were you and they were flying to turkey?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We'd take people up there, ambassadors and things like that. Once in a while we'd carry cargo that was for the embassy that was up there because Turkey was a neutral nation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But neither of you were supposably flying any military supplies, right?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No. We had an airplane that was paying within the airlines. I don't remember the name of the airlines.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Commercial airlines?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Commercial airlines, yeah. And we had civilian clothes. I had to go down to the embassy and there were times when I'd get clothes, the sleeves were down to here. They were heavy guys. But it was -- that we enjoyed. And we always had good food up there and yeah. And Ankara was, not Ankara, Istanbul was an interesting town. We got around to see that because if we were there two, three days, I was a radio operator so I never had anything to do. The mechanics would work on that airplane, but I was always taking off into Istanbul whenever I wanted to while we were there. We were only there two, three days at any one time. I think we made about four trips there at the most, but I was very fortunate. I got into Russia and Turkey and India and down south in the Khartoum.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any close calls or particularly rough missions?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Once in a while you have some problems with the plane, we flew on one engine. We were up when -- as the British moved further out in the desert, we would fly supplies in for them into Tripoli which was the furthest trip we ever went. And couple of times coming home, we'd lose an engine. And the first time that happened to us, we went back and landed and took off again. It was supposably repaired and lost and the pilot said, to hell with it, we'll fly on one engine, and after that anything like that happened, we'd fly on one engine because they were flying an airplane that was beautiful. Their still flying some of them today DC-3s, DC-4s, C-54s, a C-47.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it would fly okay on one engine?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Slower and lower it, though?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It was just a good flight. We never flew that high over the desert. Didn't have to. We were maybe 5, 6,000 feet. I don't ever remember flying over 10,000 feet and that was over the ocean. I made 13 trips from New York to Paris. We go to Bermuda four and a half hours and then ten hours to the Azores, and six-hour into Paris. But we can never fly straight into Paris because Brest was occupied by the Germans and they didn't believe the war was over. They tried to get information to them. They finally, after about a month, they sent Germans in there to tell them the war was over because the first time that we went they said you can go from the Azores straight into Paris, and all of a sudden we see shoots all around us. We never experienced anything like that. We got the hell out of there fast and we had to fly over England and come back for a while until they were able to reach the people in Brest to tell them the war was over as far as they're concerned.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: They didn't believe it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. So maybe a month or so after V-E Day, they continued to shoot at passing planes?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I don't know if it was a month or two weeks or three weeks, something like that, because it would take us a week to go and one week to come back. So it only happen to us twice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They were shooting at you?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. So after that we went around over England and came back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything else from the North African Campaign?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Just that we'd make two, three trips a day, sometimes. The further out they push, the British would push them back, the longer it would take us to go until we'd fly up to Benghazi and beyond Benghazi into Tripoli. Tripoli was the one we stayed there for a while then go back. We go back and forth in one day, but it was a long trip. Then after that, they put us on trips into Russia on a special mission into Russia and Turkey. That was interesting because we got to see countries that we never had a chance to see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things were you flying on those special trips to Russia?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: The same airplanes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Supply wise?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Not supplies so much as people.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: People?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: There were supplies, small amounts for the people who were based up in those areas. A Lot of people, when I came home, told them they wouldn't believe us that the United States had an air base in Russia during the war. They would fly from England, bomb Germany and land in Poltava. That's where where we used to go into. We brought supplies throughout those people there and then, from there we'd go all the way back again to Kiroba. The British would turn around and bomb Italy and bomb Bulgaria and land in Italy and then bomb France and land in England again. So they were making like a big triangle, and all we ever flew up there were supplies or to people back and forth. In case somebody got sick, they had to take a crew member or something like that. That's what we did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So more diplomats and that sort of thing you were flying, or were they soldiers?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Once in a while, very few soldiers. The British were able to fly from there into Russia. When I came home and told them we had an air base with Russia, nobody believed me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where about would that be in Russia?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Poltava.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Poltava? That would be in Ukraine?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Ukraine area, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Interesting. Didn't know about that at all.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: A lot of people don't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you continued -- you were based in North Africa. Did you move at all after that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No. Well, after two years, I was flown out of the whole area down at Khartoum and Sudan and over into India and Carachi, Yemen, you mentioned, Burine Isle (ph). You mention the place, I was there. But when I came home, they put me on New York to Paris and I made 13 round trips there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you come home and do that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: After two years overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So sometime in 1944 maybe?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: '43, '44, yeah. I got out the end of '44, so yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were -- you got out before the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, no. I was in the Air Force until '45, the end of '45.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay, all right.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: But when I came home, I asked them to ground me there because I was able to get my wife. My wife worked for the government in Cleveland and she was able -- very easy for her to get a transfer to the Air Force base where I was. So I asked if I could be based there and not fly. I worked in navigation and briefing because I did all that flying for several years overseas. And they said, no, they cant do that. If I don't want to fly, then they can send me to the Battle of the Bulge. So I started to laugh. I said I'll fly. I don't know if they really would have done that, if they were just talking, but my guess is, at that time I was a young guy and I believed them. But when I think back, I think they were just talking. I like to think that's all they were doing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But at that point, at the end of 1944, they were doing that.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. So I made 13 round trips from New York to Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you started flying those in early 1945?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, through '44 and part of '45, too, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How often were those trips?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It would take us a day or one flight, not a day. We would fly from Wellington to New York and that's where we picked up our cargo or passengers and go to Bermuda. The third plane in was ours to go to the Azores, and then again, the third plane to Paris, and coming back, it was the same thing; every third plane. So sometimes we were lucky. One time there was a big storm and the planes who were leaving from Paris got to the Azores but they couldn't get to Newfoundland because the weather was so bad. And the reason they went to Newfoundland, it was a long trip going west from Bermuda. Well, they couldn't fly that far east so they would fly to Newfoundland which was a shorter trip. And that's how they were, why they were when we were first there we couldn't -- never figured out why we were going around that big circle. And it didn't dawn on us until later on when I was almost out of the Air Force that somebody was talking about it because it was a longer trip coming east, going west and you're going against the wind. But it took me all those years to figure that out, to hear that story. We never figured it out ourselves. But that was what it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you can fly a longer distance when you were flying west?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Because the wind is behind you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because the wind is only --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. I get that. Makes perfect sense.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Today it doesn't matter because they go up over 30,000 feet. We never went over 10,000 feet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you really had to take into consideration what it was doing?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Oh, yeah, sure. But it never dawned on us. We never learned about it until after. I think it was a while. I was out of the service already and I heard some guys talking about it, and I stopped to listen, and it made sense to me. And that's the reason why we didn't we go from Paris to Bermuda. Well, because it was too far and you couldn't fly that far against the wind.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But those missions go okay? Did you have any trouble on those crossings?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Never. You fly a DC-3 or a DC-4, we never had a problem. There was one occasion we lost an engine going from Tripoli to Cairo, so we went back and they fixed it and we took off again, and the engine cut out and the pilot said, hell with it, we'll fly on one engine. And you could. We did that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The C-47s, they called it the flying boxcars, didn't they?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Oh, beautiful. They're still flying some of these down in South Africa. Not south Africa, but in South America. Their using those down there. It's a great airplane.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call? Getting letters from your wife? Anything like that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Sometimes I would get mail, somebody would go home and then come back. They would bring mail. I would send mail that way with guys leaving Cairo. There were times that she get the mail in just a couple days, and then a month later she'd get the mail that I written a month before. It all depends who was going and who was carrying it. Mail was just crazy kind of stuff all the time. But I wrote everyday, she wrote everyday, and you get -- sometimes I get a letter she written in May, I wouldn't get it until July and vice versa, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: If we were lucky, the guy I gave it to carried it all the way back to the States and put it in the mail that day. She would get it in two, three days, you know. So it was all crazy stuff, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you write to each other?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I wrote to her everyday.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What sort of things would you talk about?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Just tell her where I've been, what I've seen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you tell her where you had flown?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I never discussed any cities or anything, but I've been in the Middle East and you know. Yeah, I would tell her. It was rarely mentioned, the name. We weren't supposed to. Although, I know the guy that was reading my mail never read my mail, so I could have written anything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why didn't he read your mail? Wasn't that his job?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That's his job, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But he didn't?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: He was a navigator and he did a lot of flying himself, and we were all good friends and we knew each other and knew who was honest and who wasn't. So that was one of the things. There was a time, I remember when I was called into Cairo to see some civilian. I don't know what they were. I think they were looking for guys to tell on other people who were cheating or lying or something like that. I said if I ever see anybody that I know is a spy, I'll let you know but I'm not going to report on a guy every time, once a week on what he's doing and where he's going and things like that. I just -- I'm not one of those kind of guys. And I never met anybody that I felt was suspicious of any kind. So I turned them down and I said, if I find somebody that is suspicious, then I'll turn them in, but otherwise, I can't be a spy and report on them, everything they do which is what they wanted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They wanted you to report on a fellow crew member or --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Different people. They picked out certain people and they'd have me spy on them and write down what they're supposed to be doing or what he's talking about. And I just -- most of the guys that I knew there, I felt very comfortable with them. And they wanted me to tell them about everything, about what these guys were doing, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Obviously they wanted you to work in Intelligence?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That's what these people were. They were not in the service, they were in the Intelligence. The whole separate, today it's what, CIA or something. Yeah, it didn't matter whether they were doing something wrong or not. I'd have to write what they were doing everyday and I just -- I couldn't do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the enticement? Were they going to offer you more pay or they just wanted you to do that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And this would be the 'ole assets (ph) maybe, I don't know, whatever it was.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I don't remember what the CIA or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think it was the OSS.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: It could have been at that time, yeah. I said if I ever find somebody that I think is being crooked or isn't being honest about something or spying, I'll let you know. But I'm not going to -- I can't report every single thing he's doing, who he's talk to and everything like that. I just didn't feel comfortable with it. And most of the guys that I knew, there weren't that many people because I was flying so much, they never got to be too close. Three or four people really, that I was very close with. One guy slept across from me, one right next to me, one on the other side, and we were very close friends. And three of them are gone already. There's one still alive out there, out west. And we still keep in touch from time to time, but it's -- can't do those things now. I'm not a spy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do much with those buddies as far as entertainment during -- between missions, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Well, I was the only one that flew. So they were there all the time, and when I'd come back and I'd have two, three days off, they were working. And I would go down, see the pyramids. I'd go down the different areas. I love history, ancient history. And that was an opportunity, don't quit, you know. So even if I had to go by myself, I go. I'd get a ride into town and then from there, I'd take one of their local buses, the local bus, or whatever, you know. And I did that as much as I could. And once in a while, I'd bump into somebody who's also interested in doing something, who happened to be going through. And we'd go out together there. But most of the time I was on my own.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Those places you visited, they were intact? They weren't bombed or anything?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No, no, no. They were the pyramids, no. There was really no attacks in Egypt at all. Not while we were there anyhow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not a military importance?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I guess not. I don't know that that's always an excuse for not to bomb or something, but their -- the British were very good, they kept the Germans away. And little by little, they pushed them back. We used to fly supplies in for them, shelves and things like that. And every time we went on a trip it was a little bit further so we covered that whole desert all the way up to Tripoli.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Little by little.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: After about two years. I came home in '44, beginning of '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And did the missions to Paris?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: And then I did Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And then you were finally discharged in late '45?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, December.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long had it been? I guess you saw your wife probably in '44, right?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: When I came home, yes. I brought her up there. She worked for the government in Cleveland, so it was easy for her to get transferred to the airfield. She worked at the airfield and every time I'd come back, we were together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's nice.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We'd take time off, we'd go to Philadelphia and New York. I missed getting in Japan because we were home that one time and we went up to Philadelphia, and when we came back two days later, the whole base was empty. I said, where did everybody go? There was no planes on the field or anything. They were all taking McArthur into Japan, so I missed that trip. But I was with her, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I didn't miss it. At that time, I didn't care. Although, when I think back, it would have been nice to go all over the Middle East, Russia, Turkey, that whole area. But I was never really anywhere else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you on V-E Day, then? Were you back in the States or were you in Paris?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: What was the date.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: May 8th of 1945? Early May.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I was home. I was home at the end of December '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were probably on the safe side. When do you remember celebrating victory in Europe at all? They say you were based near New York right at that point.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I was in Wellington, Delaware.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Delaware, okay. I mean you see the pictures of the exciting celebrations on V-E Day.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I think -- when was that? That was in '45?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, May of '45.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Okay. I was discharged in December --

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Of '44, I think.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, you --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you don't remember the celebrations or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: I can look through here and see if you could find them or something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War Two, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Just how lucky I was. Wherever I was, I was never shot at. One time we were shot at and it was a mistake on the part of somebody. We used to fly from New York to Bermuda and then the third plane in was ours in Bermuda to the Azores and same thing. Well this one trip, we come to the Azores and they said, you guys can go straight in now to Paris. You don't have to go all the way around England and come back because the Brest has been taken over by the Americans. And what happened was that for a while, the first time they told us it was opened, you can go over there. They were shooting at us. There were shots all over. The first time we've ever been shot at, we didn't know what the heck was going on, but we got the hell out of there fast. They never -- the Germans that were in the corner of Brest didn't believe that the war was over until they sent Germans in to tell them that it was over. So when we first went across, they said, you're okay now. The Germans surrendered. Well, they didn't tell the Brest people that. They couldn't get loose to them or they didn't believe it or whatever it was. So we were the first plane to go up there, and we went over Brest and all of a sudden, the shot. We were lucky __+. And we got the hell out of there as fast as we could but they wouldn't believe it, so. But then after, they sent Germans in there to tell them then it was -- that we'd go straight in so. Sometimes you got to be lucky.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, very good. Maybe we should take a look at the photo album here.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. And they came into Egypt, and we flew in from one base to the other bases. Jack Benny, and there were a couple others, couple women there. I got some more pictures there. I can't remember the name.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to Jack at all?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Oh, sure. He flew with us, yeah. As a matter of fact, when he came back to Cleveland to play out way out east here, there was summer theater. I don't know if you were old enough to remember that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Kenley Playhouse, or whatever that is?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: No, no. That was something else, further east. But this was in -- all the way out Lee Road. Not Lee Road, the next one, Richmond Road. And he was there, and so I went back stage and I brought him these pictures, and he said, come in, I want to talk to you. And he was changing clothes and he let me bring my son in so he could -- my wife couldn't come in because he was changing clothes -- so he could talk to us because he remembered being there in Cairo. There were several of them there, but they were very good, and we flew them around from one base to another so they can entertain the troops.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, we were lucky. Then we flew people up to the Tehran Conference with Roosevelt and who was in charge of Russia at the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These are great. So you bought these series of pictures?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah. Well, they gave them to us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, they gave them to you?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's fantastic.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We flew them up there. We didn't fly the President. Somebody else took him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's a great little souvenir.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: We flew the other people that were going up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: So they give us this thing. But I did meet, what's their name, from China. She's not in there. Well, they met with the Chinese, too, but that meeting was in Teheran and then Cairo first. And so when I happen to be in navigation, when she got off the airplane, I went out there and shook hands with her. What was her name? She was running the whole -- her husband was a big official, but she was the one that was doing all the talking and was always meeting --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: From China?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Boy, I don't know. I mean, I just know Chiang Kai-Shek.

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: That's his wife.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: His wife?

sp.speaker: Norton Norr
sp.p: Yeah, Madame Shek. (END OF CD)
